newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albanians struggle to cope with life under curfew.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albanians struggle to cope with life under curfew.

text.p: The streets of Tirana grow more tense each evening as darkness falls and battered cars compete with horse-drawn carts and fast-moving pedestrians in a frenzied dash for cover.
It is not the prospect of violence that frightens Albanians but the arrival of a strictly enforced curfew.
The curfew starts at 8 p.m. and ends at 6 a.m. It was ordered by the all-party government in early March at the height of the national emergency.
It turns Tirana into a ghost town each evening when the pot-holed streets packed just moments earlier suddenly empty.
"The curfew is a real drag," said 19-year-old Denada Kuzumi. "I hardly get to see my boyfriend anymore. After work I have to hurry right home. It is total stress."
Nearly 300 Albanians have been killed in the violence that has swept Europe's poorest country in the last two months following the collapse of fraudulent get-rich-quick investment schemes.
The curfew has helped restore a semblance of order, but greatly changed the lives of ordinary Albanians.

"It is very bad for business," said Arben, the depressed owner of a once-popular central Tirana cafe. "I am losing a lot of money with this curfew. Normally the place is full at 8 o'clock. If this curfew lasts much longer, I may go bankrupt."
The owner of a popular pizza restaurant said his monthly profit has fallen to $2,000 from $4,000 since the curfew effectively eliminated his evening customers.
"It's a hardship," he said. "At night I sit at home and watch the news. But that just makes me angrier."
CURFEW INITIALLY WELCOMED

Many Albanians in Tirana at first welcomed the curfew because it reduced the intensity of nightly gun battles once so frightening that even the capital's hungry stray dogs ceased their nightly chorus of howls.
But the gunfire has since subsided to an occasional burst of machinegun fire.
An eight-nation security force made up of 6,000 troops from Austria, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Romania, Spain and Turkey is arriving on a mission to secure humanitarian aid to isolated areas.

"We are stuck at home watching television now," said Edmond, a 25-year-old unemployed lawyer. "I used to stay out in the bars with my friends until after midnight. Not anymore. I miss my friends so much."
Attempting to adapt to the curfew, one disco changed its hours to between 2 p.m. and 7 p.m but most people don't want to go dancing in the afternoon.
"If you want to have some fun now you have to go to a club and stay there all night until the next morning," said 21-year-old Sonali Daci. "But that is too long for me. There is no place to sleep."
THE BENEFITS
With Tirana's flourishing nightlife in abeyance many Albanians have discovered that sleep is not such a bad thing after all.

"We go to sleep earlier now," said Arben, a 35-year-old lawyer who shares a two-room flat with his wife and their three-year-old son. "But that has a good side -- we make love more often. We sleep better."
An unemployed man named Artan said he missed the discos but has got to know his fiancee better.
"The curfew is good and bad," he said. "We stay with each more at night and have more sex, but on the other hand, we cannot go to the discos and bars and drink with our friends."
Liqeni Artificial Park in western Tirana fills with parked cars in the hour before the curfew.

It has always been a favourite spot for couples. Before the curfew they would wait for the cover of darkness, now there is no time. They are oblivious to the children who play outside their cars in the late afternoon sunshine.
Not all Albanians complain about the curfew.
Suzana, an unemployed 45-year-old with two children, said it had improved her quality of life.

"My husband stays more with me and the chidren at home," she said. "He drinks less. He wants to drink, but I can keep him under control at home. And even if he gets drunk he sleeps in his bed, unlike before when either friends brought him home or he slept on a bench outside somewhere."

Teuta Frasheri, a 36-year-old travel agent, said her husband brings home a different sort of problem -- work. He is a workaholic computer programmer and brings home with him what he can't finish at the office.
"I hate being cooped-up in the house in the evenings now that days are getting longer," Frasheri said. "My daughter misses playing with her friends."
Sanie, 45, said her husband's business selling spices imported from Bulgaria was suffering because of the curfew.

"He is losing a lot of money, but on the other hand, we see him more," she said. "Unlike before he stays with the children. Before they almost never saw him. He came late and left early. They should keep the curfew."
